title: Medicare Advantage Overpayments: What to Know

payload.title: Medicare Advantage Overpayments: What to Know
payload.excerpt: Sicker seniors are leaving Medicare Advantage at higher rates than healthy enrollees, a trend tied to overpayment practices and network restrictions that can limit care access.
payload.author: David Haass
payload.seoTitle: Medicare Advantage Overpayments: What Seniors Should Know
payload.seoDescription: Learn how Medicare Advantage overpayments affect coverage and why sicker seniors are switching plans. Compare your options with confidence.

structuredSections.text: Introduction: The Hidden Story Behind Medicare Advantage Overpayments

structuredSections.content: A pattern has emerged in recent Medicare research that deserves your attention: seniors with the most complex health needs are leaving Medicare Advantage plans at higher rates than healthier enrollees. This trend connects directly to how private insurers get paid for covering you, and it raises real questions about whether plan marketing always matches the coverage experience once you actually need frequent care.

Understanding the link between plan payment structures and your day-to-day coverage can help you avoid an unwelcome surprise later. This article walks through what overpayments are, why sicker beneficiaries are switching plans, and how to compare your options with more confidence. If you are weighing [Medicare Advantage](/medicare-advantage/) against [Original Medicare](/original-medicare/), understanding these dynamics can help you make a more informed decision.

structuredSections.text: What Are Medicare Advantage Overpayments and Why Do They Matter to You

structuredSections.content: Medicare pays private insurance companies a set monthly amount for each person enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan. That payment is adjusted based on how sick or healthy the government expects you to be, a process known as risk adjustment. Insurers report diagnosis codes to Medicare, and higher documented risk generally means a higher payment.

In some cases, coding practices have led to payments that do not accurately reflect a beneficiary's actual health status. Federal watchdogs, including the HHS Office of Inspector General, have flagged billions of dollars in improper risk adjustment payments tied to unsupported diagnosis coding. Organizations such as the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) and KFF have also published research and analysis examining the scope and impact of Medicare Advantage overpayments.

structuredSections.calloutTitle: Why This Matters to Taxpayers and You
structuredSections.calloutText: Overpayments affect more than federal budgets. They shape how insurers design plan benefits, networks, and cost sharing, which can directly influence the coverage choices available to you.

structuredSections.text: Why Sicker Seniors Are Disenrolling from Medicare Advantage

structuredSections.content: Recent analyses from organizations such as KFF and MedPAC have found that beneficiaries with multiple chronic conditions or high care needs disenroll from Medicare Advantage and switch to Original Medicare at notably higher rates than healthier members. This pattern suggests that once a plan's real-world limitations become apparent, some seniors decide the coverage no longer fits their situation. If you are considering a change, it helps to understand the [Medicare Advantage disenrollment period and other switching rules](/medicare-advantage/enrollment-periods/) before you decide.
Network restrictions are a common factor. Prior authorization requirements, referral rules, and limited specialist access can slow down care for people managing serious or multiple conditions.

This gap between how a plan is marketed during enrollment season and how it performs when you actually need extensive care is worth taking seriously. It does not mean Medicare Advantage is the wrong choice for everyone, but it does mean your specific health needs should guide the decision, not just the advertised premium.

structuredSections.calloutText: If your health needs are complex or likely to change, it helps to review your plan's prior authorization and referral rules closely, not just its monthly cost.

structuredSections.text: Medicare Terms and Plan Types Can Feel Confusing When You Are Comparing Options

structuredSections.content: Original Medicare includes Part A for hospital care and Part B for medical services, and it lets you see any provider who accepts Medicare nationwide. Medicare Advantage, also called Part C, is offered through private insurers and often includes extra benefits, but typically requires network use and prior approval for certain services. Medigap policies work alongside Original Medicare to help cover out-of-pocket costs like coinsurance and deductibles. If you take Original Medicare, you may also want to review your [Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage](/medicare-part-d/) options separately, since Original Medicare does not include drug coverage on its own.

Overpayment and risk adjustment issues connect to plan design because insurers have financial incentives tied to how your health risk is documented. This does not mean your care is compromised, but it does explain why plan benefits and restrictions vary so widely between insurers.

A simple way to think it through: if you value flexibility to see any provider and predictable costs, Medicare Supplement Plan G paired with Original Medicare may fit better. If you prioritize lower premiums and added benefits and are comfortable with network rules, [Medicare Advantage](/medicare-advantage/) may be worth comparing closely.

structuredSections.text: Uncertainty About Costs and Coverage When Your Health Needs Change

structuredSections.content: Out-of-pocket costs can shift quickly once you develop a new diagnosis or need more frequent specialist visits. A plan that looked affordable at enrollment can become expensive fast if copays add up across multiple appointments, tests, and treatments.

A low monthly premium does not always mean lower total costs. Medicare Advantage plans carry a maximum out-of-pocket limit, which according to CMS.gov is capped at $9,250 for 2026, but reaching that limit through frequent copays can still strain a fixed income.

structuredSections.title: Questions to Ask Before Switching Plans
rows: What is the copay for specialist visits, diagnostic tests, and hospital stays?
Is there a separate deductible for drugs, and how does it compare to the 2026 Part D maximum deductible of $615?
What is the plan's annual out-of-pocket limit, and how does it apply to your typical care needs?
Which services or medications require approval before you receive care?
structuredSections.footnote: Costs vary by plan and location, so always confirm current details directly with the plan, CMS.gov, or a licensed agent.

structuredSections.content: I always tell people to look past the premium and check the plan's out-of-pocket maximum and specialist copays first. Those numbers tell you the real story of what happens if your health needs increase, which is exactly when good coverage matters most.

structuredSections.text: Protecting Your Doctors, Prescriptions, and Peace of Mind Before You Switch Plans

structuredSections.content: Before making any change, confirm that your current doctors and specialists are still in-network under the plan you are considering. Networks change from year to year, even within the same insurance company.

Review the plan's prescription drug formulary closely, since medications can move between cost tiers or require prior authorization. A drug that was affordable last year may cost significantly more under a different plan's formulary. This is especially important to check within your [Medicare Part D plan](/medicare-part-d/) or your Medicare Advantage plan's drug benefits.

items: Call your doctors' offices to confirm which plans they currently accept
Check the plan's drug formulary for your exact medications and dosages
Compare total annual costs, not just monthly premiums
Ask about referral requirements for specialists you already see

structuredSections.content: Comparing plans based on your specific care needs, rather than general advertising, reduces the risk of an unwanted surprise once you need care. A licensed agent can walk through these details with you and clarify your choices without pressuring you toward a particular plan. If your circumstances qualify, you may also be able to make changes outside the standard enrollment window through a [Special Enrollment Period (SEP)](/medicare-advantage/enrollment-periods/).

structuredSections.calloutText: Licensed Medicare agents are expected to explain plan differences in plain language and disclose plan availability transparently, which can make comparing options far less stressful.

structuredSections.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Medicare Advantage Overpayments and Switching Plans

faqs.question: I want to review my options, but I am not ready to talk to anyone yet. Is that okay?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to research on your own is a normal and healthy part of choosing coverage. Use trustworthy resources to build your understanding first, and reach out to a licensed agent only when you feel ready for a conversation.

faqs.question: Will I get a pushy sales call if I ask about my plan options?
faqs.answer: Licensed agents are expected to explain your options clearly without pressuring you toward a decision. Transparent, no-obligation help means you can ask questions, compare plans, and take your time before deciding anything.

faqs.question: Can I figure out Medicare Advantage overpayments and plan changes on my own?
faqs.answer: Self-research is valuable and worth doing, especially to understand basic terms and trends. A licensed agent can still help fill in gaps around specific plan rules, network details, and formulary changes that general research may not fully cover.

faqs.question: How do I know which sources I can trust when researching Medicare Advantage plans?
faqs.answer: Look for plain-language explanations, transparent licensing information, and clear disclosures about plan availability. Checking reviews and testimonials from real clients can also help you gauge whether a source or agent is trustworthy before you make a decision.

structuredSections.text: Conclusion: Making a Confident Choice as Your Health Needs Evolve

structuredSections.content: Understanding overpayments and disenrollment trends gives you a sharper lens for evaluating Medicare Advantage plans, especially if your health needs are complex or likely to change. Comparing coverage based on your doctors, prescriptions, and total budget, rather than the premium alone, helps you avoid surprises down the road.

When you feel ready, licensed help is available to walk through your specific situation without pressure. Taking a thoughtful, informed approach now can help you choose coverage that holds up when you need it most.

keyTakeaways: Medicare Advantage insurers receive payments adjusted through risk adjustment based on documented diagnosis codes
Federal watchdogs like the HHS Office of Inspector General have flagged billions in improper risk adjustment payments
Beneficiaries with multiple chronic conditions disenroll from Medicare Advantage and switch to Original Medicare at higher rates than healthier members
Prior authorization requirements and network restrictions can slow care access for people with complex health needs
Reviewing a plan's prior authorization and referral rules is as important as comparing monthly premiums
